opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because Go is almost the perfect case where the inductive bias of a convolutional network lines up with the structure of the problem. The board is a 19-by-19 grid, the rules are translation-invariant, and a lot of what matters tactically is local: liberties, shapes, ladders, eyes. So a ResNet-style convnet, like the ones used in AlphaGo Zero and KataGo, gets a lot for free. You're baking in the assumption that the same pattern means roughly the same thing anywhere on the board, and that makes it very sample-efficient and very compute-efficient per forward pass.

Transformers make the opposite bet. They assume very little about spatial structure, and every position can attend to every other position from the first layer. In principle that's attractive for Go, because some of the hardest parts of the game are global: life-and-death fights spanning the board, ladders that run corner to corner, whole-board judgments about influence versus territory. A convnet has to build up its receptive field layer by layer to see those interactions, and sometimes it doesn't quite get there. Some of the famous failure modes of strong Go engines, like the adversarial attacks that exploit weird cyclic group situations, arguably come from the network not representing long-range structure robustly.

So the tradeoff in my mind is something like this. At small to medium scale, with a fixed compute budget, convnets are really hard to beat in Go, because the prior is so well matched. As you scale up data and compute, the transformer's flexibility starts to pay off, and you can learn whatever spatial priors you need instead of hard-coding them. That's the same story we saw in vision with ViTs versus ResNets: below a certain scale the convnet wins, above it the transformer catches up and often overtakes.

There's also a practical systems angle. Go engines run the network inside a search loop, MCTS, many thousands of evaluations per move. Latency and throughput per evaluation really matter, and convolutions on a small fixed grid are extremely efficient. A transformer with 361 tokens isn't crazy expensive, but attention is quadratic, and you're paying that cost on every node of the search tree. So even if a transformer is a slightly better evaluator per call, the search might do better with a faster, slightly weaker convnet that gets more playouts.

What I find more interesting philosophically is that with self-play the data is essentially unlimited, so the usual argument for strong inductive biases, that you're data-constrained, mostly goes away. You become compute-constrained instead. Then the question is which architecture turns FLOPs into playing strength most efficiently, and that's an empirical question that probably shifts as hardware and scale change. My guess is that the long-run answer looks like hybrids: convolutional or local processing early to cheaply capture shape, plus some global attention to handle the board-wide reasoning convnets struggle with. That seems to be where a lot of architectures land once you take both the problem structure and the compute budget seriously.

r001.rationale: It says a convnet must build its receptive field layer by layer to connect global interactions and may not get there.

r002.rationale: It says every position can attend to every other from the first layer, which supports distant board-wide connections.

r003.rationale: It says transformers may need more scale to learn spatial priors, but does not state that they require more training data specifically to learn local invariances.

r004.rationale: It gives no report about Eric Jang’s own attempts or whether he has succeeded in making transformers outperform ResNets for Go.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a fun one because Go is kind of the textbook case where the inductive bias of convolutions looks like it should win, right? You have a 19 by 19 grid, the rules are translationally invariant, local patterns like ladders and eyes and ko shapes matter a lot. So AlphaGo, AlphaZero, KataGo, they all went with ResNets, and that was the obvious call at the time.

The way I think about the tradeoff is that convolutions are basically a transformer where you've hard-coded the attention pattern to be "look at your neighbors." That's a great prior when data is scarce. But Go has these very non-local interactions, like a group's life depends on a liberty on the other side of the board, or a ladder that runs across the whole thing. A convnet has to stack a lot of layers to get that receptive field, and even then it's doing it through a kind of lossy relay. A transformer can just attend directly from one corner to the other in a single layer.

The catch is that transformers are data-hungry and compute-hungry, and in the self-play regime you're not actually data-limited, you're compute-limited per game. So the question becomes: for a fixed inference budget during MCTS, which architecture gives you a better value and policy estimate? And historically the convnet won that fight because it's so much cheaper per forward pass, and the search compensates for the architectural weaknesses.

What's changed my view a bit is seeing how well transformers scale when you just give them more. If you believe the bitter lesson, you should expect the less opinionated architecture to eventually win, and I think that's been true in basically every other domain. Vision was the holdout and then ViTs caught up. So my prior is that Go goes the same way once someone actually spends the compute, and some of the newer engines are hybrid or attention-based for that reason.

But honestly, I think the more interesting takeaway isn't about Go. It's that Go is a case where we knew the right inductive bias and it still only bought us a constant factor. That tells you something about how much to trust your own priors about structure in a domain versus just letting the model learn it.

r001.rationale: It explains that distant Go interactions require many convolutional layers to reach and are passed through a “lossy relay.”

r002.rationale: It says a transformer can attend directly between opposite corners of the board in one layer.

r003.rationale: It calls transformers data-hungry and says convolutional priors help when data is scarce, but does not clearly explain that transformers need more training data specifically to learn local invariances.

r004.rationale: It discusses the historical advantage of convnets and predicts transformers may eventually win, but does not report whether Eric Jang has succeeded in making transformers outperform ResNets for Go.

astra-6.text:
I think the tradeoff is largely about how much structure you want to build in versus how much you want the model to learn. A convolutional network has a useful inductive bias for Go: local patterns matter, and a pattern you recognize in one part of the board often matters elsewhere. That can make it quite efficient with data and compute.

But Go also has these long-range interactions. Whether a group is alive can depend on something happening across the board. A transformer gives you a more direct way to connect those distant positions, whereas a convolutional network has to build those relationships through multiple layers.

That doesn’t automatically make the transformer better. The board is small and fixed, so convolutions are a pretty strong fit. I’d want to compare them at a fixed compute budget, including the cost of running the network during search. A more expressive network isn’t necessarily a stronger Go player if it means you can afford substantially less search.

r002.rationale: It says a transformer offers a more direct way to connect distant board positions.

r003.rationale: It discusses CNNs’ data efficiency but does not state that transformers need more training data to learn local invariances.

r004.rationale: It does not report whether Eric Jang has succeeded in making transformers outperform ResNets for Go.

sol-6.1.text:
For Go, convolutional networks have a very useful inductive bias: the same local pattern can matter in different parts of the board, and convolutions let you share that computation efficiently. A transformer has to learn more of that structure, but it can connect distant parts of the board directly. That’s useful because a fight in one corner can affect whether a move on the other side is good.

So I’d frame it as a tradeoff between having the right prior and having a more flexible architecture. With limited data and compute, I’d expect the convolutional bias to help. At a much larger scale, attention might make it easier to learn global relationships. But you have to compare the whole system: if one architecture is more expensive per position, you may get fewer search simulations for the same compute budget. A better policy network doesn’t automatically make a stronger Go player.

r001.rationale: It says convolutions share local patterns and contrasts this with transformers connecting distant board regions; it does not explain that CNN local receptive fields make distant battles difficult to connect.

r002.rationale: It says a transformer can connect distant parts of the board directly, such as linking a fight in one corner to a move on the other side.

r003.rationale: It mentions limited data and compute favoring convolutional bias, but does not state that transformers need more data to learn local invariances.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim about Eric Jang’s results or whether transformers have outperformed ResNets for Go.
